segments.text: Euclid's Elements, Book One, Proposition Thirty-Four. In a parallelogram, opposite sides and opposite angles are equal, and the diagonal bisects the area. Let A C D B be a parallelogram, with A B parallel to C D and A C parallel to B D, and let B C be its diagonal. We prove that the opposite sides and opposite angles of parallelogram A C D B are equal, and that the diagonal B C bisects the area.

segments.text: Since segment A B is parallel to segment C D, and the transversal B C falls upon them, by Proposition Twenty-Nine, the alternate interior angles A B C and B C D are equal. Again, since segment A C is parallel to segment B D, and B C falls upon them, by Proposition Twenty-Nine, the alternate interior angles A C B and C B D are also equal.

segments.text: Thus triangles A B C and D C B have the two angles A B C and B C A equal to the two angles D C B and C B D respectively, and the adjoining side B C common. By Proposition Twenty-Six, angle-side-angle congruence, their remaining sides and angles are equal: side A B equals side C D, side A C equals side B D, and angle B A C equals angle C D B. Furthermore, since angle A B C equals angle B C D and angle C B D equals angle A C B, by Common Notion Two, adding equals to equals, the whole angle A B D equals the whole angle A C D. Finally, since side A B equals side D C, side B C is common, and angle A B C equals angle B C D, by Proposition Four, triangle A B C equals triangle D C B. Therefore in any parallelogram, opposite sides and opposite angles are equal, and the diagonal bisects the area, as was required to prove.
